fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "A single scripture written in the constellations", "body": "Chance Garton opens with David Warner Mathisen, whose site starmythworld.com collects years of work arguing that the world's myths are one scripture written in the constellations. Mathisen traces his own start to childhood nights watching stars with his father and to H.A. Rey, the Curious George illustrator whose 1952 book The Stars, A New Way to See Them redrew the constellation outlines. That outlining system, he says, is what makes the mythical connections visible, and without it the same stars hide them. Chance has begun with Star Myths of the World Volume Four, on Norse mythology."}, {"title": "The jailed preacher who said it two centuries ago", "body": "Mathisen insists he is not the first to notice this. He points to Plato hinting at it, to Christmas carols full of stars and heavenly host, and above all to Robert Taylor, a preacher of the late 1700s and early 1800s who drew large crowds in London, spent three years in jail for it, and left behind The Devil's Pulpit and a separate set of astronomico theological lectures, both searchable on archive.org. Mathisen thinks the term astrotheology comes from Taylor. Chance adds Godfrey Higgins and Anacalypsis, which argues the same universal system from the etymology side."}, {"title": "Why the knowledge disappeared and who benefited", "body": "Much of the hour asks why this vanished. Mathisen ties Taylor to the French free thinkers, the revolution of 1789 and the American break of 1776, when Benjamin Franklin pushed to outlaw inherited titles and dismantle feudalism, a system held in place not only by castles and armed men but by a literalist church teaching that lords ruled by divine decree. Chance argues the ecclesiastical order was the machinery that funneled land and wealth upward. Mathisen cites economist Michael Hudson on how oligarchy struck back, and compares the star system to kung fu, powerful and good but capable of being hijacked."}, {"title": "Ships, bows, dragons and the ark of the waters", "body": "Chance drives a long riff on language. The ship of state leads to the constellation Argo and its prow, to bow as both arc and weapon, to arche and archon meaning head and ruler. He notes the Viking dracar, the Greek dracon, and the Chinese dragon boat whose word for dragon is long, links he thinks nobody arranged on purpose. Mathisen answers that myths everywhere are handed down in verse, stylized measured language built on metaphor and double meaning. Both then read the ark, from Moses to Perseus to Sargon of Akkad, as the boat of the female generative power carrying a seed."}, {"title": "Myths as maps back to the buried self", "body": "Mathisen's answer to why we need myths at all is psychological. Drawing on Peter Levine, Gabor Mate and Richard Schwartz, he describes trauma as separation from self, an unconscious survival move a small child makes and then forgets. The myths dramatize exactly that, he says, in babies set adrift in arks, in Osiris cut into fourteen pieces, in Jesus in the tomb, in Inanna stripped and hung in the underworld, and every one of them comes back. Chance connects this to his sound healing work locating stuck energy in the biofield, and Mathisen ends on John Michell's Twelve Tribe Nations."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: The stellar scholar and prolific author David Warner Mathisen joins InnerVerse to discuss the ancient universal system, codified in the stars above. Join us as we explore the origins of all myths, religious texts, and perhaps even some star stories that are disguised as "ancient history."
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the Plus+ Extension we discuss the Hercules constellation, chaos, and the storm gods of the world. We also get into a deep speculation about what the technology of star myth might mean about the nature of the universe, and the possibility of great cycles in which consciousness expands and contracts.
